title: Plant responses: effect of light or gravity on seedlings
aim: To investigate the effect of light from one direction on the growth of newly germinated cress seedlings, by measuring their height and observing the direction in which they grow.
background: Plants respond to their environment by growing in a particular direction. A growth response to light is called phototropism, and a growth response to gravity is called gravitropism (or geotropism). Shoots grow towards light (positive phototropism) and away from gravity (negative gravitropism). Roots grow towards gravity (positive gravitropism).

These responses are controlled by a plant hormone called auxin, which is made in the tips of shoots and roots. When light comes from one side, auxin builds up on the shaded side of the shoot. In shoots, auxin stimulates cell elongation, so cells on the shaded side grow longer than those on the light side and the shoot bends towards the light. This helps the plant absorb more light for photosynthesis.

In a root lying horizontally, auxin builds up on the lower side because of gravity. In roots, high concentrations of auxin inhibit cell elongation, so the upper side grows more than the lower side and the root bends downwards. In this practical, cress seedlings are grown in three conditions: light from one side, light from above, and total darkness. Seedlings grown in the dark grow tall, thin and yellow because they cannot make chlorophyll without light.
hypothesis: Cress seedlings given light from one side will grow towards the light, seedlings given light from above will grow straight up, and seedlings kept in the dark will grow straight up but taller and paler than the others.

variables.independent: Direction of light the seedlings receive (light from one side, light from above, or no light).
variables.dependent: Direction of growth (angle of bending from the vertical) and mean height of seedlings (mm).
control: Same number of cress seeds per dish (10)
Same type and amount of cotton wool, and same volume of water added each day
Same temperature for all dishes (kept in the same room)
Same type of cress seed from the same packet
Same light intensity and colour for the lit dishes
Same length of time for growth (8 days)

equipment: Three Petri dishes (without lids) or small containers
Water and a 10 cm³ measuring cylinder
Three cardboard boxes, one with a slit cut in one side
method: Label three Petri dishes A (light from one side), B (darkness) and C (light from above).
Place the same amount of cotton wool in each dish and add 10 cm³ of water to each so the cotton wool is moist but not flooded.
Count out 10 cress seeds and spread them evenly on the cotton wool in each dish.
Leave the dishes in a warm place with light from above for 1 to 2 days until the seeds germinate. Record how many seeds have germinated in each dish.
Measure the height of each seedling with a ruler and calculate the mean height for each dish (day 0 of the treatment).
Place dish A inside a box with a slit cut into one side, facing a lamp or window, so light only enters from one side.
Place dish B inside a completely closed box so it receives no light.
Place dish C in an open box, or under a lamp directly above, so light comes evenly from above.
Keep all three dishes in the same room so the temperature is the same. Add the same volume of water (2 cm³) to each dish every day.
Every two days, measure the height of each seedling in mm with a ruler (from the cotton wool to the top of the shoot) and calculate the mean height. Note the colour and direction of growth.
On the last day (day 8), use a protractor to measure the angle between each seedling in dish A and the vertical, and calculate the mean angle.
Record all results in a table and draw a line graph of mean height against time for each condition.

safety.risk: Hot bulb could cause burns, or a fire if it is near cardboard; electricity near water.
safety.precaution: Use an LED lamp, keep it a safe distance from the box, keep water away from the lamp and plug, and switch it off when the room is empty if possible.

safety.risk: Some seeds bought for gardening are treated with fungicide, which could be harmful if swallowed.
safety.precaution: Do not eat the seeds or seedlings, and wash hands after handling them.

safety.hazard: Scissors or craft knife used to cut the slit
safety.precaution: Cut on a cutting mat, away from the body, or have the slit cut by the teacher.

headers: Dish A, light from one side: mean height (mm)
Dish C, light from above: mean height (mm)
results.notes: Observations on day 8: dish A seedlings were green and bent towards the slit, with a mean angle of 42° from the vertical; dish B seedlings were tall, thin and pale yellow and grew straight up; dish C seedlings were green, short and sturdy and grew straight up. All 10 seeds germinated in dishes A and C, and 9 in dish B. Plot mean height (y-axis) against day (x-axis) as a line graph with one line for each condition.

analysis: Seedlings in dish A, with light from one side, bent towards the light (mean angle 42° from vertical). This is positive phototropism. Auxin built up on the shaded side of each shoot, causing cells on that side to elongate more, so the shoot curved towards the light.

Seedlings in dish C, with light from above, grew straight upwards because auxin was distributed evenly, so cells on all sides elongated equally. This dish acts as a control to show that bending in dish A was caused by the direction of light.

Seedlings in dish B, in darkness, grew the tallest (mean 48 mm on day 8) and were pale yellow. Without light they could not make chlorophyll, and they used stored food in the seed to grow rapidly upwards. They grew straight up because the only directional stimulus was gravity: shoots show negative gravitropism.

The mean height of the dish A seedlings increased from 4 mm on day 2 to 31 mm on day 8, a mean growth rate of 4.5 mm per day. Note that the heights in dish A are measured vertically, so bent seedlings may be longer than their measured height.
The results support the hypothesis. Using 10 seedlings per dish and calculating a mean reduces the effect of variation between individual seedlings.

errors.error: Bent seedlings are hard to measure, so their measured height does not represent their true length.
errors.improvement: Measure the length along the curve with a piece of thread then measure the thread, or photograph the seedlings next to a ruler and measure the image.

errors.error: Light may leak into the dark box or through gaps in the box for dish A, so light is not truly from one direction.
errors.improvement: Seal the boxes with tape and line them with black paper, leaving only the slit open for dish A.

errors.error: Cotton wool may dry out at different rates, so water availability varies between dishes.
errors.improvement: Add the same measured volume of water to each dish every day and keep the dishes at the same temperature.

errors.error: Some seeds may not germinate, so dishes may have different numbers of seedlings.
errors.improvement: Sow extra seeds and thin them to the same number, or record the number that germinate and calculate means from the seedlings present.

examTips: Learn the terms: phototropism (response to light) and gravitropism or geotropism (response to gravity). Shoots are positively phototropic and negatively gravitropic; roots are positively gravitropic.
Explain bending using auxin: unequal distribution of auxin causes unequal growth. In shoots, more auxin on the shaded side means more cell elongation there.
Remember that auxin has opposite effects in shoots and roots: it stimulates cell elongation in shoots but inhibits it in roots.
Always identify the control: the dish with light from above (or all round) shows what happens without a one-sided stimulus.
Seedlings in darkness are tall and yellow because they cannot make chlorophyll and use stored food to grow upwards. Do not say they are 'dead'.

questions.question: What is phototropism?
options: A growth response of a plant to gravity
A growth response of a plant to light
The process by which plants make glucose using light
The movement of water through a plant
markScheme: 1 mark: a growth response to light
questions.explanation: 'Photo' means light and 'tropism' means a growth response to a stimulus from one direction. Gravitropism is the response to gravity, and photosynthesis is how plants make glucose.

questions.question: Which plant hormone causes shoots to bend towards light?
markScheme: 1 mark: auxin
questions.explanation: Auxin controls phototropism and gravitropism. Gibberellins are involved in seed germination, ethene controls fruit ripening, and insulin is an animal hormone.

questions.question: Explain how auxin causes a cress shoot to bend towards light coming from one side.
acceptedAnswers: cells on shaded side elongate more
markScheme: 1 mark: auxin builds up (moves) to the shaded side of the shoot
1 mark: auxin causes cells on the shaded side to elongate (grow longer) more
1 mark: so the shaded side grows faster than the light side and the shoot bends towards the light
questions.explanation: The bending comes from unequal growth. Auxin does not make cells on the light side shrink: the shaded side simply grows more.

questions.question: A seedling is laid on its side in the dark. After two days its root has bent downwards. What is this response called?
markScheme: 1 mark: positive gravitropism (geotropism)
questions.explanation: The root grows towards the pull of gravity, so it is positively gravitropic. It cannot be phototropism because the seedling was in the dark. Shoots show negative gravitropism by growing upwards.

questions.question:
The heights of 10 cress seedlings on day 8 were (in mm): 28, 32, 30, 35, 29, 31, 33, 30, 27, 35.
Calculate the mean height.
questions.explanation: Add all ten heights (310 mm) and divide by the number of seedlings (10), giving 31 mm.

questions.question:
The mean height of seedlings in dish A was 4 mm on day 2 and 31 mm on day 8.
Calculate the mean rate of growth between day 2 and day 8 in mm per day.
markScheme: 1 mark: increase = 31 − 4 = 27 mm over 8 − 2 = 6 days
1 mark: 27 ÷ 6 = 4.5 mm/day
questions.explanation: Rate = change in height ÷ time. The time is 6 days (from day 2 to day 8), not 8 days. Dividing 27 by 8 gives the wrong answer of 3.4 mm/day.

questions.question:
A student planted 20 cress seeds and 17 of them germinated.
Calculate the percentage of seeds that germinated.
What is the purpose of dish C, in which the seedlings receive light from above?
options: To show what happens to seedlings with no light
To provide extra seedlings in case some die
To act as a control, showing that bending in dish A is caused by light coming from one side
To test the effect of gravity on roots
markScheme: 1 mark: it is a control, for comparison, showing seedlings grow straight when light is not from one side
questions.explanation: Seedlings in dish C grow straight up. Comparing with dish A shows that the bending is caused by the direction of light, not by something else such as the type of seed. Dish B is the one with no light.

questions.question: Give two variables that should be kept the same for all three dishes.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: number of seeds; volume of water added; temperature; type of seed; amount of cotton wool; length of time
questions.explanation: These variables affect germination and growth, so they must be controlled. Only the direction of light should differ between the dishes.

questions.question: Explain why 10 seeds are planted in each dish rather than just one.
markScheme: 1 mark: individual seedlings vary (and some may not germinate)
1 mark: so a mean can be calculated, reducing the effect of unusual seedlings and giving more representative results
questions.explanation: One seedling could be unusual or fail to grow. Measuring many and calculating a mean gives a more reliable picture of how seedlings respond.

questions.question: How would seedlings grown in complete darkness for 8 days most likely compare with seedlings grown in light from above?
markScheme: 1 mark: taller, thinner and yellow (pale)
questions.explanation: Without light, seedlings cannot make chlorophyll, so they are yellow. They use stored food from the seed to grow rapidly upwards. They grow straight up, not sideways, because there is no light from one side.

questions.question: A root is placed horizontally. Explain why it grows downwards.
acceptedAnswers: auxin inhibits cell elongation in roots
markScheme: 1 mark: auxin builds up on the lower side of the root because of gravity
1 mark: in roots, auxin inhibits cell elongation
1 mark: so the upper side grows more than the lower side and the root bends downwards
questions.explanation: The key difference from shoots is that auxin inhibits elongation in roots. More auxin on the lower side means the lower side grows less, so the root curves downwards.

questions.question: Suggest how a student could measure how much the seedlings in dish A had bent towards the light.
markScheme: 1 mark: use a protractor to measure the angle between each shoot and the vertical
1 mark: measure several seedlings and calculate a mean angle (or photograph and measure the angle on the image)
questions.explanation: The angle from vertical is a quantitative measure of bending. Photographing seedlings allows careful measurement without damaging them.

questions.question: Describe a method to investigate the effect of light from one direction on the growth of cress seedlings.
markScheme: Indicative content: put the same amount of cotton wool in three Petri dishes; add the same volume of water; put the same number of cress seeds (for example 10) in each; allow to germinate; measure starting heights; place one dish in a box with a slit so light comes from one side; one in a closed dark box; one with light from above (control); keep at same temperature; water each dish with same volume daily; after several days measure heights with a ruler and calculate mean; measure angle of bending with a protractor; record colour and direction of growth; repeat

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method that would give valid results, including setting up the different light conditions, a control, how growth and direction are measured, and at least two control variables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most key steps, but some detail of measurements or control variables missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as putting seeds near a light and observing them, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers describe how one-sided light is achieved (a box with a slit), include a control dish, explain what is measured (height, angle, colour) and list control variables such as water, temperature and number of seeds.

questions.question:
After 8 days, seedlings with light from one side were bent towards the light, seedlings with light from above were straight and green, and seedlings in the dark were straight, tall and yellow.
Explain these results.
markScheme: Indicative content: one-sided light: auxin builds up on the shaded side, cells there elongate more, shoot bends towards light (positive phototropism), helping it absorb more light for photosynthesis; light from above: auxin evenly distributed, equal elongation on all sides so shoots grow straight; dark: no light so no chlorophyll made, so yellow; seedlings use stored food to grow tall quickly; grow straight up because the only directional stimulus is gravity (negative gravitropism of shoots)
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains at least two of the three results using auxin distribution and cell elongation, with correct reference to phototropism or gravitropism.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes the results or states that shoots grow towards light, with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Explaining means giving the mechanism: unequal auxin leads to unequal elongation. The dark-grown seedlings also show that shoots respond to gravity by growing upwards.
